questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a refactor without a check actually risks
questions.learningObjective: name the risk created by restructuring code that nothing observes
questions.stem: A 400-line pricing routine is being restructured. Nothing about it is under check, and the change will touch twelve of its branches. The work is booked for Friday afternoon with no automated check to run afterwards. What risk is being taken?

options.text: The change is unverifiable, because a refactor is judged by behaviour that nothing here observes, so a silent defect ships as tidier code
The change is slow to review, because a reviewer can only judge a routine this long by reading all of it from end to end
options.misconception: reduces the risk to reviewer effort and ignores the unobserved behaviour

options.text: The change is hard to undo, because a large diff in one commit cannot be reverted without losing the whole afternoon's work
options.misconception: names the cost of reverting rather than the cost of not knowing

options.text: The change will merge without conflict, because a refactor that moves no data cannot collide with another branch's work
options.misconception: believes a behaviour-preserving refactor is free of risk by construction

questions.explanation: A refactor is defined by a promise that behaviour is unchanged, and the only way to know whether that promise held is to compare behaviour before and after. With no check, the comparison never happens, so the twelve touched branches are reviewed by eye while the thing that would catch a mistake is the thing being refactored. The trap is that a clean-looking diff reads as evidence: a reviewer sees the same twelve branches in a tidier arrangement and has nothing to weigh against the change. Option C is real but it is the cheap risk, since a revert restores the old behaviour rather than certifying the new one. Option D confuses merge conflict with correctness, which is the risk a refactor is famous for not having, until the code it moved had a defect nobody could see.
questions.hint: Ask what a refactor promises, and what would tell you whether the promise held.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The smallest step that makes a refactor checkable
questions.learningObjective: choose the first step that turns an unverifiable refactor into a verifiable one
questions.stem: The pricing routine has no check around it and the team has two hours before the Friday slot. What is the smallest step that would make the refactor verifiable rather than merely tidy?

options.text: Record what the routine returns for a fixed set of inputs today, run that unchanged, and only then move any code
Move the routine into a new module first, so the refactor will have a clean boundary to work against afterwards
options.misconception: believes a new boundary is what makes behaviour observable

options.text: Run the refactor on a branch and compare its output with the deployed version by hand for two inputs
options.misconception: accepts a two-input manual comparison as though it were a check

options.text: Cut the change into four smaller commits, so that if one of them is wrong the other three still land
options.misconception: confuses smaller commits with an observation of the result

questions.explanation: The gap is not that the refactor is large, it is that nothing compares before with after, and the cheapest thing that closes that gap is a set of recorded answers to run twice. It has to be recorded before the code moves, because afterwards the only source for what the old code did is memory, which is what the team is trying not to rely on. Option B makes the code tidier to navigate and leaves the observation gap exactly where it was. Option C is the honest fallback when no time exists for writing checks, and its weakness is arithmetic rather than principle: two inputs cannot cover twelve branches, so a defect in the tenth branch is invisible and the branch looks refactored. Option D is worth doing anyway, and it is not the same thing at all: a commit boundary controls how a mistake is isolated, not whether it is found.
questions.hint: Ask what would be run before the code moves and again after it, and choose that.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a month of defect data says about an unchecked refactor
questions.learningObjective: weigh defect counts after a refactor as evidence without overreading them
questions.stem: A 400-line pricing routine was restructured in one commit on a Friday with no automated check. In the following month 6 defects were reported against pricing, and 4 of the 6 sit in branches that commit touched. What does that evidence support?

options.text: That the refactor is a plausible contributor, since most of the reported defects are in code it changed, and that is not yet proof
That the refactor caused the defects, since 4 of the 6 reported defects are inside the lines it changed
options.misconception: reads a majority of reports as a demonstrated cause

options.text: That the refactor is sound, since only 2 of the 6 defects fall in code it did not touch at all
options.misconception: treats the untouched share as a clean bill of health

options.text: That the defects are unrelated to it, since a routine with no checks has no baseline to compare the reports against
options.misconception: uses the missing baseline to dismiss a plausible signal entirely

questions.explanation: Four of six landing in touched branches is a strong hint and not a demonstration, because the same concentration would appear if the refactor had simply moved attention and review onto the code it rewrote. Without a check there is no counterfactual: nobody can say what those four branches would have produced in the month before, so the number supports an investigation rather than a verdict. Option C is the mirror-image error, and its arithmetic is what gives it away: the two untouched defects say nothing about the four touched ones, so citing them as clearance treats absence of evidence as evidence of absence. Option D names a real limitation, missing baseline, and then uses it to dismiss the signal that survives without one. The honest next step is a recorded comparison for the four branches, not a decision either way.
questions.hint: Ask what the count would have looked like if the refactor had not happened, and whether anyone knows.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Recording behaviour that is known to be wrong
questions.learningObjective: explain what a check that pins current wrong behaviour does and is for
questions.stem: A legacy report drops the last order of every day. Before fixing it, a check is added that asserts the report lists every order except the last. What has the check established?

options.text: Only what the code does today, which is its purpose: it pins the wrong answer so that changing it becomes a visible diff
That the report is correct, since a passing check is a statement of intended behaviour written in executable form
options.misconception: believes a passing check certifies the behaviour as intended

options.text: That the report will be fixed, since writing the wrong answer down gives whoever fixes it an unambiguous target
options.misconception: believes pinning current behaviour is what triggers the fix

options.text: That the report cannot change, since any later edit will now be caught by a check that passes today
options.misconception: believes a passing check forbids every subsequent change

questions.explanation: A characterization check is a photograph, not a specification: its job is to make the current answer durable so that a later change to the code shows up as a difference. Once the last order is pinned as missing, deleting that skipping step produces a failing check and a diff that says exactly what changed, which is worth more than a paragraph of prose describing the defect. Option D is the belief that makes teams avoid writing these checks, and it inverts the purpose: a check exists to fail when behaviour moves, so a passing check is an invitation to change rather than a fence around it. Option C confuses a record with a request. The check can be written without knowing the right answer, which is the whole reason this pattern works on code nobody has read.
questions.hint: Ask what the check compares: the code against itself, or the code against a specification.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The limit of what a recorded answer proves
questions.learningObjective: state what a passing characterization check leaves undetermined
questions.stem: A characterization check was written for a legacy rate calculator by tracing it, and it passes. The team now says the calculator is understood. What does a passing characterization check leave undetermined?

options.text: Whether the behaviour is the intended behaviour, since the check records what the code does and never what it should do
Whether the behaviour is recorded at all, since a passing check by definition exercised that path at least once
options.misconception: doubting that a passing check has recorded anything

options.text: Whether the behaviour will hold tomorrow, since a check written today cannot describe a later change to the code
options.misconception: confuses a record of the present with a guarantee about the future

options.text: Whether the calculator is understood, since a check produced from a trace is a specification in another form
options.misconception: believes tracing the code and stating the requirement are the same act

questions.explanation: The check was derived from the code, so it can only ever be as right as the code was. A rate calculator that has been quietly rounding the wrong way for six years produces a passing check that pins the wrong rounding, and from that moment the defect is defended by a check rather than merely undocumented. That is the boundary of the pattern and the reason the recorded set is normally handed to whoever owns the requirement, to mark which answers are wanted. Option C is a different worry and a real one: the check constrains the next change, which is exactly what it is for. Option D is the seductive error, because a trace and a specification look identical once written down, and the only thing separating them is where the statements came from.
questions.hint: Ask where the expected answers came from, and what that source cannot tell you.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Tracing a date routine whose month table never learned about leap years
questions.learningObjective: trace a routine that carries its own month lengths and never receives the year
questions.stem: A scheduler advances dates with its own table and is never told the year. The table is [31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]. The routine is DEFINE addDays(m, d, n): d <- d + n. WHILE d > LENGTHS[m - 1]: d <- d - LENGTHS[m - 1]. m <- m + 1. RETURN m * 100 + d. The scheduler runs in 2024. Trace addDays(1, 20, 45) and state what it returns.

options.text: 306, because the table spends 28 days on February and lands one day later than the real March date
305, because the routine applies the true length of February for the year it was asked about
options.misconception: assumes a routine holding its own table consults the year

options.text: 304, because the routine stops subtracting once the day fits inside the first month it reaches
options.misconception: believes the loop halts on the first month whose length the day fits

options.text: 307, because the routine keeps the day inside the 28-day month and rolls the month forward anyway
options.misconception: adds a spurious day to the fall-through without following the loop

questions.explanation: Verified by running the routine and by two independent routes to the true date. Executing it: 20 + 45 gives 65, the loop subtracts January's 31 to leave 34 in month 2, 34 is greater than 28 so it subtracts 28 to leave 6 in month 3, and the routine returns 3 * 100 + 6, which is 306. The real date, computed by handing the same offset to a calendar, is 5 March, and the same answer falls out of day-of-year arithmetic: 20 January is day 20, adding 45 gives day 65, and 2024 is a leap year so the end of February is day 60, leaving day 5 of March, which encodes as 305. The routine is one day out, and it will be one day out in every leap year and correct in every other one, which is why a characterization check that pins 306 would be recording the defect rather than the calendar. Note the trap in option B: the routine is never told the year, so it cannot possibly produce the right answer for a leap February, and no amount of care in the loop body can supply what the signature omits.
questions.hint: Step the day count down month by month, then check the result against a real 2024 calendar.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a rename has to be split into steps that each build
questions.learningObjective: explain what small-step renaming buys over a single sweep
questions.stem: A field is renamed across 34 references in a codebase whose full check takes 45 minutes. One team proposes a single commit changing all 34. Why is doing it in small steps safer than as one sweep?

options.text: Each step is verified on its own, so a mistake surfaces after one step rather than after thirty-four references have moved
Each step is quicker to type, because splitting a rename spreads the same characters across more commits
options.misconception: counts keystrokes rather than the cost of an undetected mistake

options.text: Each step builds faster, because a build only has to recompile the files the individual step changed
options.misconception: believes the check would be shorter rather than repeated more often

options.text: Each step is easier to describe, because a short commit message can summarise a smaller change
options.misconception: credits the history wording rather than the observation between steps

questions.explanation: The expense of a rename is not typing, it is the interval between the first mistake and the first evidence of it, and a sweep stretches that interval across all 34 references. Done in steps, each step is a landing point where the check has run and passed, so the search for the mistake is bounded by one step rather than by the whole rename. The cost is honest and worth naming: 45 minutes per step means a rename in steps takes much longer in wall-clock terms, which is why teams reach for the sweep when a release is close, and that is exactly the circumstance in which a rename is most likely to be abandoned halfway. Option C gets the mechanism backwards, since the point is running the check more often, not making each run shorter. A rename is the ideal candidate for small steps precisely because it is mechanical: the steps are trivially reviewable and the evidence arrives after each one.
questions.hint: Ask how long the interval is between a mistake and the check that would find it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Counting what a rename actually has to touch
questions.learningObjective: count the references a rename changes and explain what each one is
questions.stem: A field is renamed from customerID to customerId. The routine is DEFINE findByCustomer(orders, customerID): hits <- 0. FOR order IN orders: IF order.customerID = customerID: hits <- hits + 1. RETURN hits. The rename changes the parameter and the field and nothing else. How many references does the rename have to change in this routine?

options.text: 3, since the declaration, the field read and the parameter read are three separate references
2, since the two references in the condition are the only ones that name the value
options.misconception: counts only the uses and forgets the declaration

options.text: 1, since a rename follows the name from its declaration and reaches every use without being told
options.misconception: believes a rename needs a single edit and no search

options.text: 4, since the loop variable is also a reference to the field being renamed
options.misconception: counts the loop variable as though it named the field

questions.explanation: Executed against the snippet, the identifier occurs three times as a whole word: once where the parameter is declared, once as the field being read on the order, and once as the parameter being read on the right of the comparison. The count matters because it is the size of the step, and the three references fail differently: miss the declaration and the parameter becomes undeclared, miss the field and the comparison reads a different thing. The subtlety worth carrying away is that a rename of this shape can look finished and still be wrong, because renaming the parameter alone leaves the code comparing the same field to the same value, so every check still passes and the intent has been lost. A case-only rename like this one is also invisible to a compiler in languages where the two spellings differ only in case, which is why a search for the old spelling is part of the work rather than an afterthought.
questions.hint: Find every whole-word occurrence of the identifier and say what each one is.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Extracting a block whose name will not sit still
questions.learningObjective: respond to a block that resists an honest name when it is extracted
questions.stem: A 90-line method holds a 25-line block that loads a customer, applies two eligibility rules and returns a discount. A reviewer asks for it to be extracted, and three attempts at a name have each been rejected as misleading. What does that failure tell you?

options.text: That the block does two jobs, so the honest move is to leave it inline until those jobs are separated
That the block's inputs are unclear, so the next name should be longer until the reviewer accepts it
options.misconception: believes a name can be stretched until it becomes honest

options.text: That the block is too long, so the name should record how long it is so callers know what they get
options.misconception: reduces naming to a size description that says nothing about purpose

options.text: That the reviewer wants fewer lines, so extract the block and leave a comment to explain what it was
options.misconception: assumes the objection was about line count rather than the name

questions.explanation: Three rejected names is evidence about the block, not about the naming. When a routine loads a customer, applies eligibility rules and computes a discount, those are three things, and a routine that does three things has no single name because there is no single thing to name. Extraction with a bad name makes the code look tidier while moving the confusion one level up, and a reader who trusts the name will call it expecting one of the three behaviours. The next move is to split the block along the two jobs it really has, which produces two routines that can each be named, and the third rejection disappears because there is now something to name. Option D is the tempting shortcut and it is exactly how a method ends up with a comment longer than the body it explains.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate things the block does, rather than how many names were tried.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The only name that can be honest
questions.learningObjective: choose a name that states the precondition a routine actually guarantees
questions.stem: A routine sorts orders so that an order whose customer has already paid comes last. The paid flag is read from a cache that may be empty, and an empty cache makes every order count as unpaid. Which name can honestly describe it?

options.text: sortPaidLastTreatingMissingAsUnpaid, because the postcondition only holds under that reading of the cache
sortPaidLast, because a caller who supplies the cache has supplied the answer the name promises
options.misconception: assumes the caller can always supply a cache that answers

options.text: sortOrdersByPaidFlag, because naming the field being sorted on is enough to describe the outcome
options.misconception: believes naming the sorted field states the resulting order

options.text: sortOrdersForCheckout, because the caller's purpose is the only thing a name really has to convey
options.misconception: treats the name of the intended use as a description of the behaviour

questions.explanation: The routine's promise is conditional, so the name has to carry the condition. With an empty cache every order is unpaid, which means paid orders are not pushed last, which means sortPaidLast is a false claim that a caller will act on. Writing the assumption into the name moves the cost of the ambiguity from the reader to the caller, who can now see that the guarantee depends on a cache being populated. Option B is the mistake this pattern exists to prevent: it takes the happy path as the contract. The general rule is that a name may assert a postcondition only where the code establishes it unconditionally, and a missing value from an external source is a precondition the code does not establish.
questions.hint: Ask under what condition the promised ordering actually holds, and put that in the name.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Two halves that share nothing
questions.learningObjective: read shared-variable analysis as the evidence that licenses splitting a method
questions.stem: A 140-line method has a first half that validates and normalises an upload and a second half that writes a thumbnail queue. No variable is read by the second half that the first half sets, and the two halves share no local. What does that establish about the split?

options.text: That the two halves can be split with no value passed between them, leaving the result unchanged
That the two halves belong in separate deployed services, since nothing connects them at run time
options.misconception: reads a local split as a deployment split

options.text: That the method was written by two different people, since shared-variable analysis reports authorship
options.misconception: treats a property of the code as a fact about the authors

options.text: That the first half can be deleted outright, since the second half reads nothing that it sets
options.misconception: concludes deletability from independence

questions.explanation: A split is free of risk exactly when no value has to cross the new boundary, and the test for that is whether any local written on one side is read on the other. Here none is, so the two routines can be separated with no parameter list and no return value, and the result of calling them in sequence is identical. That is the strongest form of the split and it is much rarer than it looks: the moment the first half computes something the second half needs, a parameter appears and the split becomes a judgement about what that parameter means. Option B confuses two different scales of change, since sharing no variable says nothing about network boundaries and is if anything evidence against one. Option D is independence misread as dispensability, and the two are unrelated.
questions.hint: Ask whether any value written in one half is read in the other, and what that means for the new boundary.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The criterion that actually decides a split
questions.learningObjective: reject line count as the reason for splitting a method
questions.stem: A method runs to 200 lines and every statement in it concerns order totals. Splitting it into two named halves is proposed on the grounds that 200 lines is long. What is wrong with that reason by itself?

options.text: Length is not the deciding property, since a split that still passes four locals between the halves moves the length and leaves the tangle
Length is the deciding property, but 200 lines is short enough that no split can repay the review it costs
options.misconception: agrees with the rule and disputes only the threshold

options.text: Length cannot be measured, since how long a method is depends on which lines a reader counts as statements
options.misconception: denies a measure that the team has already quoted

options.text: Length is the deciding property, and two halves of a hundred lines is the accepted target for this shape
options.misconception: replaces the tangle with a numeric target that licenses nothing

questions.explanation: The number of lines measures how much text a reader must hold, and a method becomes hard to hold for reasons that a line count cannot see: seven locals that any two statements might both touch, four conditions that decide which of the others run, and a loop whose body depends on values set three levels above it. A split that leaves those four locals crossing the new boundary has moved the text into two methods and left every original difficulty in place, which is why the refactor reads as an improvement and is not one. Option D is the specific way this goes wrong in practice, because a hundred-line target is measurable and gets adopted in place of the analysis that would have justified the split. Length is worth attending to as a smell, but it is evidence to investigate, not a reason to cut.
questions.hint: Ask how many values would have to cross the new boundary, and whether that number went down.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Deciding between inlining and extracting by call sites
questions.learningObjective: use the number of call sites to choose between inlining and extracting
questions.stem: A six-line helper with a one-word name is called from exactly one place, four hundred lines away. Three other helpers of the same shape are each called from four places in the same module. What does the call-site count decide here?

options.text: That the single-caller copy should be inlined into its one caller, while the three shared ones keep their names
Nothing at all, because a helper is worth exactly the same whether one place calls it or four do
options.misconception: treats the count as irrelevant to whether a name earns its keep

options.text: Only where the copy is inlined, since a helper used by four callers is worth naming for its own sake
options.misconception: applies the rule to the one-caller case and drops the other three

options.text: That all four should be inlined, since a helper called four times gains nothing at all from having a name
options.misconception: ignores the count entirely and inlines every helper

questions.explanation: A name has to be read by everyone who calls through it, and a helper with one caller asks a reader to travel to a distant definition to learn six lines that would read better in place. With four callers the arithmetic reverses: inlining would paste the same six lines into four places, and the name now pays for itself as a label that four readers share. The count is a proxy for how much the name costs to introduce, and it is the right question to ask first, though not the last. Option B is the position that lets single-caller wrappers accumulate until every method is three lines deep, which is a different kind of damage. The remaining question, once the count is in, is whether the single caller is a place where the six lines read better inline.
questions.hint: Ask who has to read the name: one reader travelling far, or four readers at the point of use.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The case that overrides the call-site rule
questions.learningObjective: recognise when a one-caller helper must keep its name
questions.stem: A helper is called from one place, and the call-site rule points to inlining it. What would make inlining the wrong move anyway?

options.text: The single caller is a loop body that reads the name as part of its own description, so inlining deletes the explanation
The helper is short, since a short routine is always better inlined however its call site happens to read
options.misconception: applies length as though it settled the question in every case

options.text: The caller lives in another file, since a name cannot carry any meaning across a file boundary in any language
options.misconception: believes file boundaries strip meaning from names

options.text: The helper changes nothing, since a routine without side effects is always the better candidate for inlining
options.misconception: confuses absence of side effects with suitability for inlining

questions.explanation: The call-site count answers how far a reader has to travel, and it says nothing about whether the name is carrying weight at the point of use. A call that reads processEachOrder(rows) tells the reader what the loop is for; the same six lines pasted in leave a loop that does arithmetic with no statement of intent, and the reader has to reconstruct the purpose from the body. That is the case the rule has to yield to: one caller, but a caller for which the name is the documentation. Options B and D both substitute a property that is irrelevant to the decision, and C is simply false, since names are used across files precisely because they travel. A single-caller helper with a meaningless name and a caller that reads fine without it should still be inlined.
questions.hint: Ask what the call site says before the reader reaches the body, and whether the name is that sentence.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: When replacing a chain of tests with a table pays
questions.learningObjective: identify when a chain of comparisons is really a data mapping
questions.stem: A pricing routine holds a chain of fourteen tests, each comparing a product code against a fixed string and returning a fixed number. The codes and numbers are edited twice a year by a pricing analyst. What does that pattern support?

options.text: A table keyed by the code, because the mapping is data the analyst already edits and no case computes anything
A table keyed by the code, because a chain of fourteen tests is by definition a lookup waiting to be written
options.misconception: believes the length of a chain is what licenses the conversion

options.text: Keeping the chain, because a table cannot be edited safely by someone who does not write code
options.misconception: confuses where the value lives with who can change it

options.text: A table of functions, because each case should keep its own body and simply be selected by its key
options.misconception: assumes each branch already contains a computation to preserve

questions.explanation: The test for this conversion is not how many tests there are but whether each branch selects a value or computes one. Here every branch compares a key and returns a stored number, so the whole chain is a mapping that a pricing analyst already edits twice a year, in code, in the place where the mistake is easiest to make. Moving it to a table moves the same edits to a place where a missing key is visible and a wrong key is greppable. Option B is the reasoning that turns a 14-test chain into a table regardless of what is in it, and it produces tables of single-expression functions that nobody can read faster than the chain. Option C confuses location with authorship: a table is at least as editable by a non-programmer once it lives in a configuration file rather than in a source file.
questions.hint: Ask whether each branch computes a value or only names one, and who edits those values.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The case that makes a lookup table worse
questions.learningObjective: recognise branches that compute rather than select
questions.stem: A second routine also holds a chain of tests, but each branch runs its own three-line calculation instead of returning a constant, and three branches share a first line that differs only in one operator. When is a table the wrong move here?

options.text: When the branches compute rather than select, because a table of functions hides the logic without reducing any of it
When two branches share a line, because a table cannot hold a value that two of its entries have in common
options.misconception: believes a table cannot express a shared part of a calculation

options.text: When there are more than three branches, because a table stops being readable past a certain number of rows
options.misconception: invents a size limit that decides nothing about the branches

options.text: When the routine is called often, because a lookup costs an access that a chain of tests does not pay
options.misconception: argues from call frequency while the branches compute different things

questions.explanation: A table of functions moves each branch's body out of sight and replaces a visible chain with a set of small routines that have to be read one at a time, and it does that without removing a single line of logic. The chain at least shows the reader, in order, what is tested and what happens; the table shows a list of keys and makes them go find what each one does. The shared first line is the more useful signal, because it says three branches want the same shape with one variation, which is an argument for extracting the shape and parameterising the operator, not for a lookup. Option B mistakes a table of values for a table of functions, where a shared body is expressed by having two functions that both call the shared one.
questions.hint: Ask whether a branch returns a stored value or runs a body, and what the chain shows that a table would hide.

questions.topic: Tracing a chain converted to a table
questions.learningObjective: trace the behaviour a lookup conversion changes for an unlisted key
questions.stem: A charge routine is converted from a chain to a table. Before: DEFINE charge(kind, n): IF kind = "A": RETURN 10 * n. IF kind = "B": RETURN 20 * n. RETURN 30 * n. After: GRID holds { "A": 10, "B": 20, "C": 30 } and the routine is DEFINE charge(kind, n): rate <- GRID[kind] where a key that is absent yields 0. RETURN rate * n. Trace charge("D", 4) after the conversion and state what it returns.

options.text: 0, because the absent key yields 0 and the conversion removed the fall-through that used to answer 120
120, because a table lookup falls back to the last entry the chain of tests had reached
options.misconception: assumes a table inherits the chain's fall-through branch

options.text: 4, because only the count survives the conversion and the rate is dropped along with the chain
options.misconception: believes the rewritten routine stops applying a rate to the count

options.text: 80, because the table keeps the rate stored for the key one place before the missing one
options.misconception: reads a table as if a missing key resolved to its neighbour

questions.explanation: Verified by executing both versions on the same input. The chain tests A, tests B, and for anything else falls through to 30 * 4, which is 120. The table has three keys and D is not one of them, so the absent-key rule gives rate 0, and 0 * 4 is 0. The same routine on a listed key still works: charge("B", 4) takes rate 20 from the table and returns 20 times 4, which is 80, exactly what the chain returned for that key. The lesson is that the final return in a chain is usually doing real work, answering every key the author did not enumerate, and a table that lists only the enumerated keys silently gives those answers a different value. A conversion is behaviour-preserving only when the old fall-through is reproduced explicitly, which means the table needs a default entry rather than an absent-key rule.
questions.hint: Run the chain first for D, then run the table for D, and compare the two answers.

questions.topic: A number that is not a constant
questions.learningObjective: recognise a literal whose value belongs to the caller rather than the routine
questions.stem: A pricing routine holds the literal 0.20 in a method that also serves two other rate categories, and those use 0.05 and 0.12. A reviewer asks for the 0.20 to be pulled out into a named constant. What is the problem with that request?

options.text: The value belongs to one category, not to the routine, so one constant would present one category's rule as the rule
The value belongs to the routine, so naming it would hide the fact that three categories use different rates
options.misconception: reverses the ownership and blames the name for the difference

options.text: The value changes too often to name, since a constant cannot differ between two calls made in the same run
options.misconception: objects to naming on grounds of run-time variation

options.text: The method already names it by its own purpose, so a second name would only add a second thing to keep in step
options.misconception: believes the surrounding method name already documents the value

questions.explanation: A constant is a claim that one value holds for the whole routine, and here the claim is false: the same method prices three categories at 0.20, 0.05 and 0.12, so the literal is a property of the call rather than of the routine. Hoisting it produces a routine that reads RATE and returns minutes times RATE, which is tidier and wrong, and the diff will show only that a number moved. The alternative is not a better constant but a different shape: pass the rate in, or move the dispatch up so the routine is told which category it is pricing. That is the general rule behind the objection, and it is worth stating broadly: a literal that differs by caller is data, and naming it turns a parameter into a lie.

A ticket asks for the rate to be a named constant, so the change writes RATE <- 2 and rewrites the routine as DEFINE feeFor(minutes): RETURN minutes * RATE. 10, because the rewritten routine no longer reads the plan and the premium rate was its old default
options.misconception: assumes the plan argument still selects a rate after the rewrite

options.text: 2, because the constant replaces both the multiplication and the number of minutes
options.misconception: believes the constant absorbs the whole calculation

options.text: 12, because the routine now adds the constant to the minutes instead of multiplying by it
options.misconception: reads the rewrite as a change from multiplication to addition

After the change, the plan argument is no longer read at all, the routine returns 10 times RATE, and RATE is 2, so it returns 20. options.text: On the object, since a value every method needs and no method chooses is state the object should hold
In a shared static, since a value common to every instance of a class should not be stored on each one
options.misconception: reads a shared value as a reason to deny the object its own copy

options.text: In each caller's own signature, because a class should never hold a value that its callers supplied
options.misconception: believes a supplied value is permanently the caller's property

options.text: In a setting fixed at start-up, because a locale read before construction can never be changed later
options.misconception: assumes a locale can never be changed while the program runs

questions.explanation: The diagnostic is repetition: a parameter that appears in every signature of one class and is passed the same value from every caller is a property of the object, and a class whose methods all need a value is describing itself incompletely. Moving it to state removes nine parameters and seven call sites that repeat a fact the object already knows, and it lets a method that uses it be called without the caller having to remember. The two methods that ignore it are the interesting part: they show the parameter was added to a signature by reflex rather than by use, and after the move they simply stop carrying it. questions.topic: The cost of moving a value onto the object
questions.learningObjective: identify the ordering dependency created by turning a parameter into state
questions.stem: The locale is moved onto the object, set once by the constructor, and the two methods that never used it are left without a parameter. What has that change cost?

options.text: Every method now depends on when the object was built, because a value fixed at construction cannot be re-established
One extra field on each object, since storing a single reference is the price of giving an object its own state
options.misconception: counts memory as though it were the cost being weighed

options.text: Nothing at all, since a field costs less memory than a parameter did in the very same signature
options.misconception: argues from memory cost when the question is about ordering

options.text: The ability to validate the locale, since a constructor cannot reject a value a caller might once have supplied
options.misconception: believes validation moves out of reach once a value is set internally

questions.explanation: A parameter is a value each call re-establishes, and a field is a value the object holds from one moment to the next. Every method that reads the field now depends on the object having been built with the right one, which means a caller who needs a different locale can no longer simply pass it: they need a second object, or a way to change the field that the class does not offer. That is the real trade, and it is a trade rather than a free improvement, so the change is worth making when the value genuinely does not vary for a given object. The general form is that state is cheaper to pass and more expensive to vary, and the count of callers who need a different value is what decides.
questions.hint: Ask what a caller does now who needs a different value than the one the object was built with.

Sharing the common part now, because two copies of six lines is duplication by any measure that counts lines

options.text: Sharing it behind a flag, so that one builder serves both reports until the seventh line has actually arrived
options.misconception: assumes a flag is free and will never become permanent

options.text: Leaving the copies separate and recording nothing, since a deliberate duplication needs no justification at all
options.misconception: believes intent is obvious from the code that contains it

questions.explanation: The three usual arguments for sharing all fail here at once: the shared part is six lines, which is small enough to read twice, it is stable, and it is about to stop being shared because one of the two copies is scheduled to grow a line the other will not. One extra line in the class, since a method that nothing calls costs nothing at all to keep alive
options.misconception: values a method by its current call count rather than its reachability

options.text: Nothing, because a method no production code calls cannot be reached by anyone using the class

options.text: A compile failure in the check alone, since the seam lives in the check file rather than in the class
options.misconception: believes a test convenience can be added without touching the class

Whether a check needed it, since a seam becomes real as soon as a check comes to depend on it
options.misconception: counts a test as a second user of the abstraction

options.text: Whether it is declared as an interface, since a declaration is what makes a seam real to a compiler
options.misconception: confuses how a seam is expressed with whether one is needed

options.text: Whether it was added alongside a check, since that is the moment at which its cost is cheapest to pay
options.misconception: treats the timing of the addition as the thing that decides

questions.explanation: A seam is a place where the design admits a second thing, and it earns its cost from that second thing arriving: another implementation, another caller, another storage backend. The interface in the first case is used, which is why it is not speculative. The setter in the second case has exactly one user and that user is a check, so what has actually been built is a way for the class's internals to be arranged from outside, which is a real capability with a real price. questions.stem: A module pulls in a date library solely because the standard library cannot format a date in the locale the product requires, and it pins that library to one exact version. What does the dependency really record?

options.text: A known gap in the platform, pinned so the workaround cannot drift, and needing a note or it outlives the gap
A preference for a richer date library, chosen because the standard library is too plain for this job
options.misconception: reads a workaround as a judgement about the platform's taste

options.text: A requirement from the product team, since only a third-party library can be licensed for commercial use
options.misconception: invents a licensing rule to explain a technical dependency

options.text: An accident of the module's history, since nobody would choose to add a library for one formatting call
options.misconception: assumes a deliberate pin is a leftover nobody meant to make

options.misconception: names the artefact rather than the gap it stands in for

options.text: Nothing, since the platform's own release notes already record that the gap has been closed
options.misconception: assumes someone else is tracking this module's obligations

options.misconception: denies that configuration can select code by name

options.misconception: believes documentation is what keeps code alive

That the new routine is called from more than one place, since one caller cannot justify a routine at all
options.misconception: requires a second caller before any extraction is allowed

options.text: That the original method ran past two hundred lines, since a shorter method never needs splitting
options.misconception: restates a length threshold as a precondition for any extraction

options.text: That the new routine is declared private, since visibility is what decides whether an extraction is worth it
options.misconception: believes the declaration's visibility settles the value of the change

questions.explanation: An extraction is worth making when the new boundary is a small, explicable list of values, because that list is what tells a reader everything the block needs and that is exactly the knowledge the method was keeping hidden. Seven parameters crossing the boundary means the reader of the new routine has to hold seven names to follow it, and the reader of the old method has to remember that it passes all seven, so the coupling has been given a name rather than removed. The way to make the extraction pay is to reduce what crosses it, usually by letting the block own one or two of the values instead of being handed all of them. questions.topic: One team's refactor is another team's change to their code
questions.learningObjective: classify a rename by its effect on callers rather than on the diff
questions.stem: A team renames a method on a class that eleven other teams call through a published interface. The rename changes no behaviour, no output and nothing outside that team's own files. How is it classified for everyone else?

options.text: A change to their code, because the call sites are theirs even when the diff is not, and their builds break
A refactor everywhere, because a change altering no behaviour cannot break a caller that used it correctly
options.misconception: judges a rename by behaviour while ignoring the call sites

options.text: A documentation change, since a rename with no behaviour change asks nothing of a caller at all
options.misconception: believes a rename needs no action because no output moved

options.text: A feature for the owning team, since only the team holding the file is entitled to call a change a refactor
options.misconception: grants a team authority to name a change regardless of who it reaches

This is also why the two parties to a rename negotiate: one owns the file, the other owns the call sites, and a change that is safe for the first can be scheduled work for the second. Option B is the belief that makes teams ship breaking renames with confidence, and its error is treating a call site as though it were an output rather than a use of a name.

options.misconception: concludes that a deprecation period can never end

options.text: The old name removed in the same release, since carrying both names is what makes it a feature instead
options.misconception: believes holding two names is what breaks the callers

questions.topic: The readability change that moved work
questions.learningObjective: recognise that extracting a call can multiply how often it runs
questions.stem: A total is computed once per call from a rate that is read outside the loop. A refactor extracts that read into a well-named routine and calls it inside the loop, so the method reads better and returns the same number. What has actually changed?

options.text: The number of reads, which now scales with the rows rather than staying at one, and no output revealed it
Nothing observable, since a refactor that returns the same number has changed nothing a caller can see
options.misconception: treats an identical result as proof that nothing changed

options.text: The return type, since a named routine cannot return the same type the loop body produced
options.misconception: believes extracting a call changes what the method returns

options.text: The rows the loop visits, since calling a routine inside a loop can skip the final iteration
options.misconception: believes a call inside a loop can end the loop early

questions.explanation: Extraction moves a call, and where the call sits decides how often it runs, so the same two-line refactor can be free or can turn one read into one read per row. Nothing about the returned number changes, which is precisely why a review that compares outputs passes, and the cost appears only under load where the multiplied reads start to show. The fix is small once seen: read the rate into a local before the loop and pass that local to the loop body, keeping the name for the reader while restoring one read per call. The general form is that a call's cost belongs to its position, and a refactor that improves legibility can quietly change a cost that was measured once and now is measured per row.

questions.topic: Tracing a named read that moved into a loop
questions.learningObjective: trace the call count produced by a readability extraction inside a loop
questions.stem: A total is computed over three rows. Before the refactor the rate was read once into a local: DEFINE totalBefore(items): rate <- rateFor(). s <- 0. FOR i IN items: s <- s + i * rate. RETURN s. After it the named routine is called in the loop: DEFINE totalAfter(items): s <- 0. FOR i IN items: s <- s + i * rateFor(). RETURN s. rateFor() returns 2 and items is [100, 200, 300]. Trace totalAfter(items) and state how many times rateFor runs.

options.text: 1200 is returned and rateFor runs 3 times, once per row, because the call moved inside the loop
1200 is returned and rateFor runs once, because a named routine is only read on its first use
options.misconception: believes naming a call makes it run once

options.text: 600 is returned and rateFor runs 3 times, because the loop drops the first row's contribution
options.misconception: starts the sum at the second row rather than the first

options.text: 1200 is returned and rateFor runs 4 times, because the loop's final test reads the rate once more
options.misconception: counts the loop's exit test as a further call

questions.explanation: Verified by executing both routines. The loop visits three rows, and the body calls rateFor each time, so it runs 3 times and the sum is 100 times 2 plus 200 times 2 plus 300 times 2, which is 1200. The earlier version reads the rate once before the loop, so it runs once and returns the same 1200, which is why an output comparison finds nothing. The trace is the argument for comparing call counts as well as results: two functions can agree on every input and differ in what they cost, and the difference grows with the number of rows rather than staying a constant. Option D is the specific mistake of counting the loop's condition, which tests an index and does not evaluate the rate.
questions.hint: Run the loop row by row, counting the calls, and add the three contributions.

questions.topic: A performance fix that makes the code worse
questions.learningObjective: weigh the gain and the charge of caching a value on the object
questions.stem: A loop that performed 41 reads per call is rewritten to cache a value in a field, so each call now performs 1 read. The field is read by nine methods, and the cached value is only correct when the object was built during the current second. What has been bought and what charged?

options.text: 41 reads became 1, paid for with a value that is only correct under a stated condition and read in nine places
41 reads became 1, paid for with nothing, since a cached field is a strict improvement on a repeated read
options.misconception: counts only the gain and treats the cached value as always correct

options.text: 1 read became 41, paid for with a method that must recompute the value whenever the second changes
options.misconception: reverses which side of the change did the repeated reading

options.text: 41 reads became 9, paid for with a field that all nine methods must each keep up to date themselves
options.misconception: assumes the read count settles at the number of reading methods

questions.explanation: The gain is real and large, forty reads removed from every call, and the charge is specific: the object now holds a value that goes stale, it is correct only while the object was built during the current second, and nine methods read it without nine of them being responsible for it. That combination is what makes the change worth a comment rather than a revert, because a reader who finds the field six months later has no way to know that a long-lived object will read a value that was correct when it was built. The alternative is to give the object a way to refresh the value, or to keep the read where it is, and the decision between them depends on the lifetime of the object rather than on the read count alone.
questions.hint: Ask how long the object lives compared with the second in which its field was set.

questions.topic: What a comment justifying a performance fix must contain
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a comment about a performance compromise stay true
questions.stem: The cached field stays and a comment beside it explains why. What has to be in that comment for it to still be true a year from now?

The counts of reads before and after, since a bare number is what convinces a reviewer the change was worth
options.misconception: believes the number is the durable part of the justification

options.text: The name of the engineer who wrote it, since authorship is what tells a reader how far to trust it
options.misconception: substitutes trust in a person for a checkable claim

options.text: A note to regenerate the file, since generated code needs an instruction before anyone edits it
options.misconception: reads the file as generated when the question is about a compromise

questions.explanation: A comment justifying a compromise has two jobs and both are about future readers. questions.topic: The comment that goes stale against the check that does not
questions.learningObjective: compare a written claim about a value with a check that reports the value
questions.stem: A routine carries a comment saying the discount cap is 500 because the finance policy of 2023 sets it that way, and the routine returns the cap by reading a field. Which replacement keeps that knowledge from going stale?

options.text: A check that fails when the configured cap is not the one the business expects, since it reports a wrong cap
A shorter comment saying the cap comes from configuration, since naming the source is enough to keep it current
options.misconception: believes pointing at the source keeps a written claim true

options.text: A check on the routine's output for one hard-coded cap, since a check holding today's figure cannot go stale
options.misconception: believes a figure fixed inside a check is immune to change

options.text: A comment recording when the figure was last reviewed, since a date tells a reader when to start doubting
options.misconception: assumes a date makes a claim self-verifying

A check that compares the configured cap against an expected value fails at the moment they part company, which converts a stale sentence into a signal that arrives on its own. questions.topic: A workaround comment that stays true
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a comment about a workaround usable rather than misleading
questions.stem: A routine carries a comment explaining that a retry is needed because the storage driver once dropped writes. The driver fixed that three releases ago. What makes such a comment survive instead of misleading?

options.text: Naming the condition that would make the retry unnecessary and the check that fails without it, so a reader can act on both
Naming the driver and its version, since a reader who knows the version can look up whether the bug is still open
options.misconception: assumes a version number tells the reader which release closed the bug

options.text: Saying the retry must not be removed, since an explicit prohibition stops a later reader tidying it away
options.misconception: believes an instruction can substitute for a reason

options.text: Saying the retry followed a production incident, since severity is what makes a reader keep the code in place
options.misconception: leans on the history of the workaround rather than its current necessity

questions.explanation: A comment about a workaround is read by someone who wants to delete it, and the only thing that stops them is a reason tied to something they can check. The condition is checkable because it points at the defect, and naming it means the reader can look at the driver and decide. The check is the stronger half, because a check that fails when the retry is removed turns the question from an opinion into a result, and it keeps answering the question after the code has moved on and the comment has been forgotten. Option B produces a comment that reads as thorough and settles nothing, since a version number does not say whether the defect is still present. The failure mode in this story is specific: a comment that was true when written and is now false, protecting a workaround whose reason has expired.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who wants to delete the retry would have to check, and whether the comment lets them.

questions.topic: Proving a legacy guard is unreachable
questions.learningObjective: identify the evidence that justifies deleting an old defensive branch
questions.stem: A guard in a validation routine exists because a 2019 payload format once reached it. That format was withdrawn in 2020 and no client has sent it since. What is the evidence that actually justifies deleting the guard?

options.text: That the branch it protects can no longer be reached, shown by a check that fails once the guard is removed
That the guard was written in 2019, since a branch that old is old enough to be called dead code
options.misconception: treats age as evidence of unreachability

options.text: That the file has not been edited since 2021, since a file nobody edits is a file nobody depends on
options.misconception: confuses an untouched file with an uncalled routine

options.text: That the format's specification is withdrawn, since a withdrawn specification cannot be produced by a client
options.misconception: assumes a client cannot hold a copy of an old specification

Everything else in the stem is a fact about history: a date a guard was written, a date a format was withdrawn, a file nobody has edited. Those facts make the guess reasonable, and a reasonable guess is how legacy branches get deleted and how the one live path through a validator disappears. The check is cheap and conclusive: remove the guard, run the suite, and if nothing fails then the branch was not exercised by anything the suite knows about, which is the strongest statement available without a production trace. questions.topic: Tracing a retry left behind for a fixed driver bug
questions.learningObjective: trace a retry that was safe only while the driver could not half-succeed
questions.stem: A write routine retries, because a storage driver used to lose writes. It is DEFINE writeRow(row): attempts <- attempts + 1. WRITE_DB(row). IF attempts < 3: RETURN writeRow(row). RETURN "ok". The driver stopped losing writes three releases ago, and attempts starts at 0. Trace one call of writeRow and state how many rows reach the database.

options.text: 3, because the routine cannot tell a lost write from a successful one now, and it reports success anyway
1, because the driver no longer loses writes so the very first attempt always succeeds
options.misconception: believes the routine can detect a lost write and so will stop

options.text: 0, because a routine that retries three times writes nothing at all when the driver is healthy
options.misconception: reads the retry as a rollback rather than as repeated writing

options.text: 2, because the retry stops as soon as the second attempt finishes without reporting an error
options.misconception: assumes a successful write is reported back to the routine

questions.explanation: Verified by execution. The first call makes attempts 1 and writes the row, and 1 is less than 3, so it calls itself; the second call makes attempts 2 and writes the row again, and 2 is less than 3, so it calls itself again; the third call makes attempts 3, writes the row, and the test fails, so it returns ok. Three rows reach the database for one call. The retry is unconditional, so the health of the driver is irrelevant to the count: what the routine reacts to is its own attempt counter and nothing else. That is exactly why the workaround outlived the bug, because while the driver lost writes the second and third attempts were harmless, and now every ordinary transient error produces three rows while the routine reports success. The remediation is to remove the retry and let a genuine failure be reported, which is safe only once the driver cannot half-succeed.
questions.hint: Follow the attempt counter through the three calls and count the write statements, not the returns.

options.text: Reporting refunds by month, since a report has to read both halves in order to produce a total

options.text: Changing the currency a refund is issued in, since currency is a property of the recording half alone
options.misconception: assumes currency concerns only one of the two halves

options.misconception: insists on simultaneity that the twenty separate schedules prevent

Build the new module that holds deciding and recording together, with both halves still calling the old one internally
Run the same refund through both arrangements and compare what each of them records
Move the twenty importing modules across a few at a time, so no one release touches all of them
Delete the old module once the last importer has moved and the new one has served production for a stated period

Building the new module second, with the old arrangement still reachable from inside it, means the comparison in the third step is between two things that are supposed to be identical and any difference is a real finding rather than a difference of plan. questions.topic: Getting a check around code before changing its shape
questions.learningObjective: sequence characterisation, restructuring and repair on untouched code
questions.stem: A 400-line pricing routine has no check around it and is due for a restructure. Put these five actions in the order they have to happen.

options.text: Record what the routine returns today for a fixed set of inputs, and run those checks against untouched code
Restructure the routine without altering any recorded answer, running the checks after each step of the move
Ask which of the recorded answers are the ones the business actually wants, since the record needs a ruling

Fix that behaviour, now that a check holds the wrong answer in place and the fix shows as a change

Recording first is what makes that separation possible, because after the shape has moved the only record of the old behaviour is the code itself, which is the thing that has just changed. Restructuring comes second for the same reason in reverse: while every answer is still pinned, a move that does not alter an answer can be made confidently, and a move that does alter one is caught immediately. The ruling in the third step is what stops the recorded set from quietly becoming a specification nobody chose, since most of the recorded answers are right and the ones that are wrong have to be identified by whoever owns the requirement. The deliberate change and the repair come last and in that order, so the defect is visible in a failing check before it is invisible in a passing one. Repairing first would mean changing the answers while they were still unpinned.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How a refactor that changes no output still changes behaviour
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanisms by which a behaviour-preserving refactor alters production behaviour
questions.stem: Explain how a refactor that returns the same value for the same input, and passes every check, can still change what the system does once it is running in production.

answer.exemplar: There are at least three mechanisms, and none of them is visible to a check that supplies one input and compares one return value. The first is timing. A change that removes a call from a path, or moves one, alters the interleaving of two requests that used to arrive together, and a defect that required that interleaving to appear now needs a different one. Two requests in a fixed order are a different system from two requests in a variable order, and both return the same value for the same input taken alone, so a suite that exercises them one at a time cannot see the difference. The second is cost. A rate read once per call and the same rate read once per row return identical answers while issuing forty-one reads instead of one, and that shows up as contention on whatever the reads contend for, which is a change in behaviour for every other request on the same resource rather than a slower version of this one. The third is reach. A branch that nothing called may become called by a refactor that routes a new path through it, and a routine that was unreachable may become reachable, and then the code that had never run in production runs for the first time under load. What follows for practice is that the set of things compared after a refactor has to include what the code did, not only what it returned: the number of calls, the order of calls, and the set of branches taken, at the sizes and concurrencies that production has. A refactor should not be described as risk-free, because that phrase describes the comparison that was made and not the system that was left behind.

questions.explanation: A good answer here has to name mechanisms rather than assert that surprises happen, and it has to connect each mechanism to the specific thing a suite cannot observe. Timing is the strongest case because it is purely a production phenomenon that no single-input check can construct. Cost is the second because it is measurable and is usually the one that was measured before the change and never re-measured. Reach is the third because it is the one teams are least likely to think about, and it is the mechanism by which a dead branch becomes live. The closing move, that the compared set has to widen beyond return values, is what turns the explanation into something a reader can act on rather than something they nod at.
questions.hint: Ask what a check that supplies one input at a time cannot observe, and list three such things.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The short useful life of a recorded wrong answer
questions.learningObjective: explain the window in which a characterization check helps and how it closes
questions.stem: Explain why a check that records today's wrong behaviour is valuable for a while and then turns into a liability, and what the team has to do to keep it useful.

answer.exemplar: The check is a record, and its whole value is that it is falsifiable against the code: it says this is what the routine does, and here is the evidence. That is something a change needs and cannot get any other way, because the alternative is reading the code and hoping, and code that nobody has read for two years is exactly the code whose behaviour is unknown. The window closes at two moments, and they are different in kind. The first is knowledge. Once somebody who owns the requirement can say what the routine should return, the check and the requirement are two statements about the same routine that no longer agree, and every fix now breaks a passing check. That is correct behaviour and it feels like obstruction, which is why these checks are so often deleted in frustration rather than in principle. The second is shape. Once the routine is refactored for other reasons, the check is asserting a detail of an implementation rather than a property of the routine, so it will block changes that are perfectly safe and it will stop being the description anyone wants. The discipline that keeps it useful is a small one and has to be applied at the moment of writing: every recorded answer gets marked as wanted or unwanted as soon as anybody can say which, and the unwanted ones are deleted in the same change that repairs them. A check should never outlive the defect it recorded, and the test of that is whether a reader could tell from the file which answers the business depends on.

questions.explanation: The question has three parts and a good answer addresses all three: why the check is valuable, what closes its usefulness, and what the team does about it. The two closing mechanisms are what distinguish an answer that understands the pattern from one that merely praises it, because one is social, since knowledge arrives and creates a contradiction, and the other is structural, since a refactored routine is no longer what the check describes. Naming the social one matters most, since it explains the otherwise puzzling experience of a team deleting a passing check in order to fix a real bug. The closing move, marking each answer as wanted or unwanted at the moment of writing and deleting the unwanted ones with the fix, is the practical content: it keeps the check inside its window instead of hoping the window stays open.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the check wrong later on, and separate the reason that is about people from the one about code.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How many small refactors become one unreviewable change
questions.learningObjective: explain how a series of small steps loses its reviewability and what the series must carry
questions.stem: Explain how a long run of individually small, individually green refactoring steps turns into a change nobody can review, and what the run should be made to carry so that it stays reviewable.

answer.exemplar: Nothing about any single step is unreviewable. A field renamed in thirty-four places, a method pulled out under a name with two parameters, a nested test turned into an early exit: each is a diff a reader can hold in their head, each lands with the suite green, and each would pass on its own merits. The difficulty is additive and it lives in the reader rather than in the writer. After forty such steps the routine in front of the reviewer bears little resemblance to the one described in the ticket, so the reviewer cannot form the model that makes a review a review, and the only procedure left is comparing both versions line by line, which is the slowest and least reliable way to find a mistake. At forty steps of about half an hour each the writing is twenty hours of work, and the temptation is to merge it into one diff, at which point the size stops being the problem and the loss of a model becomes the problem. The answer is not fewer steps, because a bigger step is a worse step, and the steps are the reason this is safe at all. It is something for the series to carry. Each step lands alone, so the sequence can be stopped after any one of them and the system is left consistent. The branch is green at every commit, so every step is verified rather than the last one being verified. And the description states what the whole run is for, so a reviewer can hold one model of the destination and check each step against it instead of reconstructing the destination from forty diffs. A series with those three properties is reviewable at both scales, and a series without them is a rewrite wearing forty good intentions.

questions.explanation: A strong answer locates the failure in the reviewer's model rather than in the diffs, because that is the part of the story a reader is most likely to have wrong. The second thing it must do is refuse the tempting remedy, since collapsing the steps into one diff is the response teams reach for and it is what actually destroys reviewability. The three properties of a healthy run, each step landing alone, green at every commit, and a stated destination, are the constructive half and they are what the question asks for. The arithmetic is there to make the incentive concrete: twenty hours of work is a lot to abandon, and a series that could be abandoned safely is one nobody has to abandon.
questions.hint: Ask what the reviewer loses across forty diffs, and what the series can carry that one diff cannot.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What makes a boundary move cheap and another expensive
questions.learningObjective: explain what determines the cost of relocating a module boundary
questions.stem: Explain what makes one module boundary cheap to move and another expensive, using the number of importers on each side and what has to stay true during the move as the deciding facts.

answer.exemplar: The cost of moving a boundary is set by two facts and nothing else: how many callers sit on the far side of it, and whether the old arrangement has to keep working while the new one is proved. Those two facts multiply, which is why a boundary with no importers is nearly free and a boundary with twenty importers is not. Start with the count. Twenty modules each need one import rewritten, and each of them does that in its own release, so the work cannot be completed in one commit and cannot even be completed in one week. The count is also the count of places where something can go wrong during the move, and each of them is a module whose build you do not control. Now the second fact. If the old arrangement can keep changing while the new one exists, the two drift, and the drift is discovered later as a difference between two systems that are supposed to be equivalent, at which point neither is obviously right. So the cheap moves share a shape, and it is the same three moves in each case. Freeze the old side, so drift is impossible rather than discouraged. Build the new side with the old side still reachable from inside it, so the two start identical and separate afterwards rather than being born different. Move the callers by choice rather than by deadline, so every module that has not moved is still correct against something that exists. The expensive moves skip all three and pay for it in a cutover, in a window where the system is half one arrangement and half the other, and in the week afterwards spent working out which half a customer's request landed in. Worth saying plainly: none of this argues against moving a boundary that is in the wrong place. It argues for moving it in an order that has an end, and an end is a date and a count going down.

questions.explanation: The question asks for a model, and a model has to be usable on a boundary the reader has not seen, so the answer has to reduce the cost to facts that can be counted before any work starts. Naming the two facts and saying they multiply is the part that generalises; a reader who has those two can price any move. The second half is what makes it a design answer rather than an observation, because the three moves follow from the second fact and can be applied without further analysis. The closing move, that this is an argument for a dated end rather than against moving, is what keeps the answer from being read as a reason to leave every awkward boundary where it is, which is the way this advice usually gets misused.
questions.hint: Reduce the cost to two countable facts, then say what the second one forces you to do about drift.

questions.topic: Naming the risk and the check for an unchecked refactor
questions.learningObjective: name both the risk of an unchecked refactor and the single check that resolves it
questions.stem: A 400-line pricing routine is being restructured and has no check around it. Name what the refactor puts at risk, and the one check that would show whether it did.

options.text: Behaviour that nothing observes, and a check asserting what the routine returns today for a fixed set of inputs
The build, and a check that the project still compiles, since a refactor that does not compile has clearly failed
options.misconception: names compilation as though it were a statement about behaviour

options.text: The schedule, and a check that the routine's runtime is unchanged, since a slower routine is a failed refactor
options.misconception: treats speed as the definition of a refactor's success

options.text: The reviewers, and a check that the diff stays under 400 lines, since a smaller diff is easier to approve
options.misconception: substitutes a measure of reviewability for a check on behaviour

questions.explanation: The risk and the check are the same fact seen from two sides, and saying both in one option is what makes the pairing correct. What is at risk is behaviour that nothing observes, which is not a vague worry but the precise reason a refactor is unverifiable: a refactor's promise is that behaviour is unchanged and only a comparison can test it. The check has to assert what the routine returns today for a fixed set of inputs and has to be run before the code moves, because after the move the only remaining record of the old behaviour is the code that was just changed. Option B is the check teams reach for because it exists already, and it is worth naming what it can and cannot do: a build proves the code is well formed and says nothing about whether it computes what it computed, which is why a refactor can be perfectly green and still be wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what a refactor promises, and what would test whether the promise held.
