questions.topic: Naming where a caller-specific value really comes from
questions.learningObjective: identify the owner of a caller-varying value and the change that makes the code say so
questions.stem: One routine holds the literal 0.20 in a method that also serves two other rate categories, and those use 0.05 and 0.12. Name where that value really comes from, and the change that makes the code honest about it.

options.text: From the category the caller is in, and passing the rate in as a parameter so it stops posing as the routine's own
From the pricing policy document, and a named constant so the routine stops hiding which policy it follows
options.misconception: names a shared source and the same constant the value cannot be

options.text: From the caller's configuration file, and moving the literal into that file so the number leaves the source tree
options.misconception: gives a plausible second home to a value with three different values

options.text: From the routine's own default, and leaving it inline since a parameter only moves the same literal up a line
options.misconception: defends the literal by making a change that does not alter it

questions.explanation: Three values for one literal is the whole argument, and it is an argument about ownership rather than about style. The value does not belong to the routine, because the routine does not decide it; it belongs to whoever knows which category is being priced, which is the caller or the configuration the caller supplies. Passing it in is what makes the routine's contract true, and it costs one parameter on a method that is already branching on category. Option B is the request that started this, and it is wrong in a specific way worth stating: a single constant cannot be right for three categories, so naming it 0.20 makes one category's rate the routine's rate. Option C sounds tidier and is worse, since it relocates a value that still has to be different per caller and hides the branching one level further from the code that needs it.
questions.hint: Count the different values the same literal needs, and ask which side of the call owns that difference.

questions.learningObjective: name the two non-syntactic callers to check and the evidence that permits deletion

options.text: Whether a configuration file or a framework reaches it by name, and production traffic with its counter at zero
Whether the project still builds without it, and a successful build, since nothing that calls it changes nothing
options.misconception: confuses a clean build with the absence of a run-time caller

options.text: Whether it is mentioned in any documentation, and a search of that documentation, since an undocumented routine is unused
options.misconception: treats the absence of prose as the absence of callers

options.text: Whether a check covers it, and the coverage report, since uncovered code is by definition unreachable
options.misconception: reads a coverage gap as proof that nothing calls it

questions.explanation: A search finds text, so the two things worth checking are the two places where a call can exist without the text of a call: a name in a configuration file, and a framework convention that finds things by pattern or by naming rule. The evidence has to come from the running system rather than from the source, because the source is the thing that produced the uncertainty, and a counter on the routine over a period of real traffic is the only thing that observes the question directly. Option D is the trap worth spelling out, since coverage measures what a suite exercised and a routine nothing calls is exactly what a suite does not exercise, so the report is consistent with both readings and settles neither.
questions.hint: Ask where a call can live without appearing as a call, and what would observe one at run time.

questions.topic: Recording a seam that exists only for a check

questions.stem: A public method was added so that a check could set one field, and no production code calls it. Name the cost it puts on the class, and what it has to record in order to stay removable.

options.text: A published method to be supported indefinitely, and the reason for it plus the check that needs it
A published method costing one line of code, and nothing at all, since an unused method explains itself
options.misconception: values a published method by its current call count

options.text: A private field the check can no longer reach, and a public setter, since a class must expose what a check sets
options.misconception: restates the seam as though the field's visibility were the problem

options.text: A build that no longer runs without the check, and a build flag, since the seam belongs to the check file
options.misconception: believes a test convenience can avoid touching the class it serves

questions.explanation: The cost and the record are one thought seen from two ends. A public method on a published class is a promise to anyone who finds it, and its current call count says nothing about that, so the cost is indefinite and it is paid in whatever a future removal breaks. The record is the only thing that keeps the promise honest: a short note saying which check needs the method and why the class is built this way, placed where someone reading the method will see it. That note is what lets the seam be removed the day the check is rewritten or a second implementation arrives, and without it the method simply becomes part of the class's history. Option B is the belief that lets these accumulate, and it is a statement about lines rather than about reachability.

questions.topic: The first move on a method that nests four levels
questions.learningObjective: choose early exits over extraction as the first change on a deeply nested method
questions.stem: A method nests four levels: a loop over uploads, a test for the file type, another for the size, and a try around the write. Seven locals are set in the loop and read at all three inner levels. Which change comes before any extraction?

options.text: Replacing the inner tests with early exits, because the shared locals are why the levels resist splitting and an exit removes one
Extracting the try block, since the write is the only part that can fail and failure is what deepens the nesting
options.misconception: picks the failure handling rather than the depth it creates

options.text: Extracting the whole loop body, since a loop over uploads is already a unit that one call can name
options.misconception: extracts the outer level and leaves the three beneath it as they were

options.text: Gathering the seven locals into one record, since grouping the values is what removes the need to pass them along
options.misconception: believes grouping the values is what reduces the nesting depth

questions.explanation: The seven locals are what make this method hard to split rather than merely hard to read, and they are also what an extraction would have to carry, so the change that reduces depth and the change that changes the value list are different moves. Early exits do the first without doing the second: the inner tests become returns, the body of the loop is no longer indented under three conditions, and every local that was set before the tests and read inside them is now set and read at the same level. That is usually the moment the real split becomes obvious, because the code per item can finally be read as a unit. Option D is a genuinely useful change that is being asked to do a different job, since a record makes the values easier to pass and does nothing about the four levels of indentation they are buried in.
questions.hint: Ask which change reduces the number of levels without moving a single value across a new boundary.

questions.topic: Answering a reviewer who wants the duplication shared
questions.learningObjective: state the strongest available answer to a duplication review comment
questions.stem: Two report builders compute the same six totals. The product team has said the wholesale report gains a seventh line next quarter and the retail report will not. A reviewer sees the duplication in a diff and asks for it to be shared. What does the team have with it?

options.text: A stated divergence, the strongest argument for keeping them apart, and a note recording it so the next reader does not merge them
A rule about how many lines may be duplicated, which is the only thing that can settle a sharing argument
options.misconception: believes a threshold decides a question that is about the future

options.text: A check asserting the two builders agree today, which is what makes keeping the duplication safe
options.misconception: offers a pin on the duplication and calls it a safety measure

options.text: The product team's roadmap, which settles the matter only once the seventh line has actually shipped
options.misconception: reasons that a decision cannot be made before its consequence arrives

questions.explanation: The reviewer is asking a fair question and the answer is not a defence of duplication in general, it is a statement about this pair. Six shared lines is small enough to read twice, the shared part is stable, and one of the two copies has a named change coming that the other will not take, which is the condition under which sharing costs more than it saves. The second half is what makes the answer hold up: the note has to go into the code, because the next reader will meet the same two builders with no memory of this review, and a decision that lives only in a discussion is one commit away from being undone. Option D describes a way of thinking that never converges, since the roadmap can always move and the argument would reopen every quarter. The honest framing is that duplication is cheap when it is small and the copies are about to differ, and expensive in every other case.
questions.hint: Ask what is about to be different about the two copies, and where that fact has to be recorded.

questions.topic: A readable change that multiplied the reads
questions.learningObjective: decide what to do about a refactor that improves reading and worsens cost
questions.stem: A page reads a rate once and then loops over 40 rows. A refactor extracts the read into a well-named routine and calls it inside the loop, so the method reads clearly and returns the same total. The page's read count rises from 1 to 41. What should happen before it ships?

options.text: Decide whether 41 reads is affordable and say so in the code, since the diff shows no behaviour change and nothing else will
Revert the refactor, since a change that alters how much work is done is never worth making at all
options.misconception: confuses one measured cost with a rule against all trade-offs

options.text: Ship it and watch the read count, since a number that starts small will not grow with the number of rows
options.misconception: believes the read count stays fixed as the number of rows grows

options.text: Keep it unchanged, because a named routine that reads configuration cannot be hoisted out of the loop later
options.misconception: believes the call's position cannot be changed by anyone who wants to

questions.explanation: The two numbers in the stem are the argument, and they point in opposite directions: the total is unchanged, which is why nothing in the review will object, and the read count has gone from one per call to one per row, which means it will be forty-one on this page and forty-one on the next one that has more rows. There is an easy repair that keeps the name and the readability: read the rate into a local before the loop and use that local inside it, so the call happens once and the sentence about the rate still reads where the reader needs it. Option B is the reflex that throws away a good change over a cost that has not been measured yet.
questions.hint: Ask how the read count behaves as the number of rows grows, and who would notice if nobody wrote it down.
